title: Iterative Cold Divider Off EX Path
motivation:
The frozen bench core still keeps DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU in the same
combinational ALU path as ADD, address generation, branch support, and
MUL. On a Tang Nano 20K, a full 32-bit divider is a strong candidate for
the universal EX-stage critical path, yet CoreMark's timed loop is mostly
multiply, load/store, and branch traffic and should pay little or no steady
state penalty from slower divide instructions.

This makes divider extraction the highest-leverage micro-opt still missing
from the frozen bench fixture: it targets Fmax directly while preserving the
hot one-cycle behavior for the instructions that dominate CoreMark.

Replace the real combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU cases in `rtl/alu.sv`
with a small iterative divider/remainder unit that is entered only for
divide-class ALU ops. Keep ADD/SUB/logic/shift/compare, address generation,
branches, jumps, loads/stores, and MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU on the existing

In EX, detect divide-class operations, latch their operands and control,

precisely: divide-by-zero, INT_MIN/-1 overflow behavior, signed/unsigned
variants, ALTOPS behavior under formal, and the existing single-retire
RVFI/order contract. The expected win is a shorter common EX critical path
and higher median Fmax with negligible CoreMark IPC loss because DIV/REM are
cold in the benchmark's hot region.

title: RTL-only hot/cold ALU opcode split
motivation:
The current best bench result already removed DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU from the
hot one-cycle EX path, but `rtl/alu.sv` still uses a dense ALU-op encoding
and one broad result case covering common RV32I work, multiply results, and
dummy divide-class outputs. That leaves the always-hot ADD/address/compare/
shift path sharing decode and mux structure with cold M-extension cases.

A sibling-core experiment on `cores/v1` showed that this specific RTL-only
reshaping can improve fitness, while more aggressive multiplier rewrites and
source-qualified hazard logic either regressed or broke. That makes the ALU
mux shape the best-supported remaining `micro_opt` angle for the frozen
bench fixture.

title: One-Deep Store Retirement Slot
motivation:
The current bench core's biggest proven gain came from a backend-only timing
change: moving DIV/REM off the one-cycle EX path. The recent failed branch
prediction attempt showed the opposite boundary on this RTL: pulling more
decode/target work into the frontend can erase the IPC gain with Fmax loss.

The next structural hypothesis should therefore stay off the fetch path and
attack the other obvious whole-core bubble source. Today any `io_dmemReady=0`
cycle on a STORE freezes IF, ID, EX, and MEM even though the store address,
replicated data, and byte mask are already known in MEM, and CoreMark does a
steady stream of normal-RAM stores to stack, list, matrix, and state data.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a one-deep pending-store retirement slot with a direct ready-store fast
path. When an aligned STORE to normal RAM `[0x00000000, 0x00100000)` reaches
MEM and `io_dmemReady` is low, capture its byte address, replicated write
data, byte mask, and RVFI-visible memory metadata into the slot, retire that
store once, and drain the physical dmem write oldest-first after the stall.

ready. Keep MMIO / UART / CoreMark marker stores unbuffered, and treat slot
occupancy as a fence for younger memory operations and externally visible end
conditions so ordering stays exact. The key win is that younger non-memory
instructions no longer have to pay every store-only dStall cycle, which
should raise CoreMark IPC without reintroducing fetch-path timing risk.

title: Registered lookahead I-fetch replay predictor
motivation:
The current bench core still turns every `io_imemReady=0` cycle into a
frontend bubble, even though CoreMark runs under a random-stall fetch model
and repeatedly revisits a small hot text footprint. The one local predictor
attempt already taught the key negative lesson: pulling branch decode,
immediate reconstruction, and target selection directly onto the current
IF/ID path costs too much Fmax on this microarchitecture.

The most promising predictor angle is therefore not another same-cycle
branch-direction table, but a timing-clean replay predictor that hides
random iStall cycles while leaving the current fetch decision dependent only
on already-registered metadata.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small registered-lookahead instruction replay predictor in IF. On live
instruction fetches, fill a tagged replay table with the fetched word and a
predicted next-PC for that fetch PC. In parallel, generate and register the
replay candidate for the PC likely to be needed on the next cycle. When the
external imem bus stalls, IF can consume the already-registered candidate
instead of injecting a bubble, and can keep advancing through hot straight-
line or loop code when the replay metadata is correct.

EX remains the architectural source of truth: it still resolves branches,
jumps, and JALR exactly, and requests recovery only when the replayed
next-PC guess was wrong or the instruction was not replayable. This targets
the tournament's random `imemReady` loss directly, but avoids the failed
bench BTFNT shape because the current-cycle IF path chooses only between
live imem data and an already-registered replay candidate rather than doing
fresh branch decode and target adds on the fetch critical path.

title: Prune EX/MEM payload and narrow store-slot control
motivation:
The current best `bench` result already found the two large levers that pay
on this RTL: keep divide/remainder off the hot EX path, and hide some
store-only dmem stalls with the one-deep retirement slot. The failed branch
and replay experiments showed the opposite boundary: adding more fetch-side
control logic costs too much Fmax on this core.

That leaves the MEM-side control cone as the best micro-opt target. The
current store-slot path still carries redundant EX/MEM metadata and uses
always-live wide compares (`instr == 32'h0010_0073`, `addr < 32'h0010_0000`)
to drive global stall decisions.

title: Tiny MEM-stage load replay buffer
motivation:
The two successful structural changes on `bench` both stayed off the fetch
and hot EX paths: iterative DIV/REM and the one-deep store retirement slot.
The remaining backend stall source is load-side dmem backpressure. Today a
normal-RAM load freezes IF, ID, EX, and MEM whenever `io_dmemReady=0`, even
if the same aligned word was returned recently and CoreMark's 6 KB working
set is revisiting it.

That makes load-side stall hiding the cleanest remaining structural lever:
it attacks iterations/cycle without pulling new decode or prediction logic
onto the frontend path that already regressed on prior bench attempts.

observe stale data. This keeps the ready-load fast path unchanged while
targeting the next obvious IPC loss without adding MEM-to-EX load bypassing
or more fetch-side control logic.

title: Single-Slot EX-Trained Branch Folding Predictor
motivation:
The predictor experiments on `bench` have all failed for the same reason:
they improved branch behavior only by adding work to the frontend `pc ->
next_pc` cone. ID-stage BTFNT hurt Fmax by pulling decode and target
generation forward, and even tiny fetch-side target caches still cost too
much in tag-compare and target-mux depth for this FPGA.

CoreMark is still rich in hot taken loop backedges, though, so there is
likely one remaining predictor shape worth trying: recover a taken-branch
cycle without touching `io_imemAddr` generation itself.

title: Decoupled Sequential Fetch Buffer
motivation:
The current `bench` frontend still couples decode directly to the live imem
response: `if_stage` emits a combinational IF/ID bundle from the current PC,
and `hazard_unit` turns every `io_imemReady=0` cycle into an immediate bubble.
That leaves two costs on the table under the tournament's random iStall model:
isolated fetch stalls always reduce IPC, and the raw imem-to-decode path stays
in the timing cone.

The recent negative lessons only rule out fetch-side prediction and replay
structures that add tag compares, target muxing, or decode work onto the live
`pc -> next fetch` path. They do not rule out a simpler decoupling structure
that stays purely sequential and flushes on EX redirect.

title: Decode-Armed Registered Backedge Redirect
motivation:
The predictor history on `bench` is unusually clear: every attempt that put
branch decode, tag compare, target muxing, or stream control directly on the
live IF `pc -> next_pc` path regressed badly on Tang Nano 20K timing, even

become known in EX.

same-cycle frontend redirect, but a predictor that uses already-registered
information to fetch the target one cycle earlier without lengthening the
current decode-to-PC critical path.

motivation:
The current load-use interlock keys off raw IF/ID bitfields, not the

direct hazard rewrite was unsafe: `bench` currently carries those raw source
fields into RVFI, so any safe relaxation has to start by canonicalizing the
architectural source view.

title: Two-Cycle Pipelined Multiply Lane
motivation:
The remaining `bench` structural space is narrow: fetch-side ideas have mostly
been Fmax-negative, and wider MEM-side buffering or replay logic has either
regressed or failed placement. The still-untried always-hot structure is the
multiply cone in `rtl/alu.sv`, which currently builds three 64-bit products on
every EX cycle even though only one MUL-family result is ever used.

Prior lessons already bracket the local alternatives. Shared combinational
multiplier reshaping regressed, which suggests the win is not in another mux
rewrite, and high-half-only offload regressed because plain `MUL` still left
the DSP-heavy path on the common EX cone. That makes a full multiply-lane
retiming the most credible remaining structural lever.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move `MUL`, `MULH`, `MULHU`, and `MULHSU` out of the one-cycle ALU and into a
dedicated two-cycle pipelined `rtl/mul_unit.sv` that is launched from EX and
returns exactly one result into the existing EX/MEM retirement path. In the
normal build, `rtl/alu.sv` would stop synthesizing the three parallel 64-bit
multiply trees, leaving the hot EX datapath focused on RV32I arithmetic,
branch/jump resolution, address generation, and the already-offloaded divider.

Keep the design single-issue and in-order: when a MUL-family op enters EX,
latch its operands plus retirement metadata, hold younger issue until the
two-cycle result comes back, and then emit the same architecturally visible
writeback and RVFI data the current single-cycle path would have produced.
This is a stronger version of the already-proven "move cold/expensive math off
the universal EX path" strategy: unlike the failed high-half-only attempt, it
actually removes all multiplier delay from the common cycle, while the IPC
cost is bounded to one extra cycle on multiply instructions instead of on
every instruction.

title: Redirect-Hit Target Word Cache
motivation:
Predictor work on `bench` has mostly failed when it touched the live
`pc -> next_pc` cone or carried fold-repair metadata through IF/ID/EX.
The core still burns a guaranteed bubble after every taken redirect,
though, because `if_stage` forces NOP on the redirect cycle even when the
target word is hot and was fetched before. The most promising remaining
predictor angle is therefore one that only does work after EX has already
made the architectural redirect decision.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a one-entry redirect-target word cache that is trained from real,
architecturally accepted target fetches and consulted only when EX already
asserts `redirect`. On a cache hit, `if_stage` injects the cached target
instruction into IF/ID on that same redirect cycle and advances the PC to
`redirect_target + 4`; on a miss, the core keeps the existing
bubble-and-refetch behavior.

This is intentionally narrower than the failed fold and BTB-style ideas.
There is no predictor lookup on ordinary fetches, no predicted-next-PC
metadata carried through the pipeline, and no mispredict recovery path
beyond the existing EX redirect. A small invalidation path for stores that
hit the cached word keeps self-modifying cases safe while repeated
CoreMark backedges and calls can reclaim one taken-control bubble and
some redirect-time iStall exposure with much less Fmax risk.
